title: A Fuzzy Request Deserves One Shared Page
summary: When a quick request grows corners, write one shared page: what changes, who it affects, real examples, open questions with owners, and the decisions made so far.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
The request lands as a two-line Slack message: "Can we tweak the refund screen a bit? Should be quick." It looks like something you could squeeze in between two bigger tickets. Ten minutes into the thread it has grown corners. Nobody's sure which users it's for. There's an exception for partial payments. Something depends on the billing service. And there's an old decision from last year that three people remember three different ways.

This is where one shared note beats another meeting. It doesn't need to be pretty. Its job is to hold the problem still long enough for everyone to look at the same thing. Other posts on this blog cover notes that live next to meetings and decisions. This one is about the note you write at the very start, while the work is still fuzzy.

Chat spreads the context across five heads

When a request lives only in chat, each person carries a slightly different version of it. The product owner remembers the customer who complained. The engineer remembers the edge case. The designer remembers the awkward screen. QA remembers the scenario that broke last release. Nobody is wrong. They're each holding a different piece, and the thread scrolls away before anyone puts the pieces together.

A note gives those pieces one place to land. Six plain headings are usually enough:

A starting shape
  • What we want to change, in one or two sentences.
  • Who it affects, and who it doesn't.
  • Examples: one real input and the output we expect.
  • Already decided, with a one-line reason each.
  • Still open, with a name next to each question.
  • Next step and who owns it.

You can fill this in ten minutes with rough bullets. The point is that everyone edits the same page instead of keeping their own version.

Write the unknowns down on purpose

A good note lets the team skip pretending it already knows everything. Instead of forcing a final plan, write the gaps down as they are: "payment state unclear," "legal needs to check the wording," "migration size unknown," "haven't tested mobile." Once an unknown is on the page, someone can own it, answer it, park it on purpose or cut it from scope.

Basecamp's Shape Up makes this a formal part of its pitch format (Chapter 6, "Write the Pitch"). Next to the problem, the appetite and the solution, every pitch lists rabbit holes, the risks worth calling out, and no-gos, the things the team has decided not to do. The book notes that a rabbit hole sometimes needs only "a few lines of text" to patch. Spelling out what you're not doing is just as useful, because it ends the scope argument before it starts. If the work is about to change hands, the same habit makes the handoff honest about what's unknown.

Examples beat paragraphs

A vague requirement gets clearer the moment someone writes one real input and the expected result. A UI debate gets easier with a screenshot of the state before and after. A policy question gets sharper when you list two customers who should get different outcomes and say why.

Examples move the conversation from "I think" to behavior the team can check. If the work has a lot of rules, the examples in the note are a natural first draft for BDD scenarios later.

Catch decisions while they're warm

Not every decision needs a design doc. Often one line does it: "We chose option B because A delays the release and C adds support load. Decided by Lan, Tuesday. We'd revisit this if refund volume doubles."

Michael Nygard explains why that line matters in his post on documenting architecture decisions. The motivation behind decisions is one of the hardest things to track on a project. Without it, someone new either accepts a decision without understanding it or reverses it without understanding the consequences, and he wants teams to avoid both. His format is short on purpose: title, context, decision, status, consequences, one or two pages at most. In a working note, it can be a single line.

Keep it light enough that people use it

The risk is that the note becomes a new ceremony. If every small ticket needs a polished document, people will dodge writing, or write just to tick a box. Match the size of the note to the size of the doubt.

Malte Ubl's write-up of design docs at Google gives a useful test for heavier docs too. Write one when the benefits (consensus, documentation, review) outweigh the extra work, and skip it when the problem isn't really ambiguous. If a doc only says how something will be built, with no trade-offs or alternatives, the author should probably just write the code. Small changes get a "mini design doc" of 1 to 3 pages. A shared note for a fuzzy request is smaller still: start rough, then tidy only the parts people need to do the work.

Try this week

  • The next time a "quick" request grows past five messages, open a shared note with the six headings above and paste the link into the thread.
  • Put a name next to every open question in it.
  • Add one real example (input and expected output) before anyone starts building.
  • When a decision is made, add one line: what, why, who, and what would make you revisit it.

Fuzzy work rarely gets clear because one person thinks harder alone. It gets clear when the team has one page to point at, fix and add to. Once everyone can describe the work and the reason for it in the same sentence, the note has done its job, and nobody needs to polish it further.

faqs.q: What should a shared note for unclear work include?
faqs.a: Six plain headings cover most cases: what we want to change, who it affects, a real example with the expected result, what's already decided and why, what's still open with an owner for each question, and the next step.

faqs.q: Why not just keep the discussion in chat?
faqs.a: In chat each person keeps a slightly different version of the request, and the thread scrolls away. A shared note puts the pieces on one page everyone can read and edit, so differences in understanding show up early.

faqs.q: How do I keep shared notes from turning into bureaucracy?
faqs.a: Match the note to the size of the doubt. Start with rough bullets and tidy only what people need to do the work. If the problem isn't ambiguous, skip the note and just do it.
